boundary_note: Bounded first pass for the frozen Carthage record (July 5, 1861) in Operations to Control Missouri [June-October 1861]. The State troops' retreat from Boonville, the Neosho capture of Conrad's company and Sigel's retreat to Mount Vernon are context. Campaign-wide marches, returns, reinforcements and multi-action loss totals are context; they are not assigned to one record or added across records. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.rationale: No inspected return establishes matched personnel at a common opening boundary. The frozen side-specific numerical strength bounds are blank (missing_numeric_strength). No figure in this pass is adopted as a simultaneous opening force.

claims.value: The frozen force field reads Brigade and Missouri State Guard divisions with no figures; the live field reads zero. NPS says Sigel had about 1,000 and the Governor approximately 4,000. Sigel reports nine companies of the Third (550 effective) and seven of the Fifth (400) with two four-gun batteries, and estimates the enemy in sight at 3,500 besides a strong reserve (reported 4,000 the evening before). Snead gives Sigel 950 effective and 125 artillerymen with seven guns, and the Governor's line 2,600 infantry and artillery and about 1,500 mounted, with about 2,000 unarmed men sent to the rear.
claims.rationale: Effective and in-sight estimates by the opposing sides; Sigel counts two four-gun batteries while he and Snead both speak of seven pieces in action. None is adopted as a matched opening strength. The live zero is not measured absence.

claims.value: Sigel found the enemy in line on elevated ground rising from the creek, about a mile and a half off, after crossing Dry Fork Creek; his column then had to pass Buck's Branch, behind which the enemy's cavalry formed. Snead places the State line on the ridge of a prairie sloping to a creek bordered with timber and brush (the name is garbled in OCR), about nine miles north of Carthage; NPS says a ridge ten miles north.
claims.rationale: Ground described by an interested report, a participant history and a summary; distances and the creek name are not reconciled. No map verification.

claims.value: Snead says the report from Carthage on the evening of July 4 was the State troops' first intimation that an enemy was in front, and that Sigel withdrew fearing the mounted force moving into the woods, not knowing it was unarmed; NPS says the same of the unarmed recruits. Sigel says the moral effect of the mounted regiments behind his lines could not be denied, though the real danger was not great.
claims.rationale: Attributed knowledge from a participant history, a summary and an interested report; no message log inspected.

claims.value: The frozen commanders are Governor Claiborne Jackson (spelled Clairborne) and Colonel Franz Sigel. Snead says the Governor assumed command in person and deployed the line, and that Weightman rapidly reformed his line after Essig's fire halted the pursuit. Sigel ordered the artillery to open and ordered part of the troops back behind Dry Fork Creek.
claims.rationale: Command roles from a participant history and an interested report; the listed commanders do not receive automatic sole credit.

claims.value: The frozen casualty text reads 244 (US 44; CS 200); the live field reads 118 (US 44; CS 74). Sigel reports 13 killed and 31 wounded and estimates the enemy's loss at not less than 350 to 400; he also reports Conrad's company of 91 men captured at Neosho the same day. Snead gives thirteen killed and thirty-one wounded against ten killed and sixty-four wounded.
claims.rationale: Original casualty returns were not inspected; preserve totals, categories, cutoffs and differences. No canonical reconciliation or casualty-based opening count; related actions must not be added without resolving population overlap. The Neosho capture is a separate action and is not added.

open_questions: The State Guard division and brigade reports (Rains, Weightman, Clark, Slack, Parsons), Sweeny's report and maps remain deferred.

NPS/CWSAC (the live battle page and the frozen Arnold rows) is one family. Thomas L. Snead's The Fight for Missouri (Scribner, 1886) is a retrospective history by the Missouri State Guard's acting adjutant-general and Price's chief of staff, who says he was with the Governor at Booneville and Carthage; it quotes Sigel's, Schofield and Sturgis's and Price's reports and is not independent of them. Sigel's July 11, 1861 report is an interested Union account. Official Records volumes are shared containers, not additional witnesses. Report dates are not event times or proof of contemporary knowledge.
No automatic commander attribution, causal campaign score, morale/readiness number or battle/campaign double counting.
